This is not covered by `s8`: for a curve in a threefold with $h^{1,1}>1$, or in any $X$ whose products of first Chern classes do not span $H^{1}(X,\Omega^1)$, the detecting argument of `s8` says nothing, while `s9` gives the identity. What remains open is the case of a subvariety of codimension $p\le n-2$ and degree $q<n-1-p$ in a general $X$. **The residual statement, stated once, and the transcription closed, same day.** The ranges of (B) now proved on the card are three: a smooth complete intersection in any nonsingular projective $X$ (`s3`); any $Y$ when the products of first Chern classes span $H^{n-p}(X,\Omega^{n-p})$ (`s8`), which contains every subvariety of $\PP^n$ and every $X$ of dimension at most two; and the top two Hodge degrees of $Y$ for any $X$ (`s9`), which for a curve is every degree and for a surface leaves only $q=0$. What remains is codimension $p\le n-2$ with $0\le q<n-1-p$ in an $X$ for which the restriction $H^{n-1-q-p}(X,\Omega)\to H^{n-1-q-p}(H,\Omega)$ is not onto: there the lifting argument of `s9` fails and the spanning hypothesis of `s8` may fail as well. For a surface $Y$ that residual range is the single degree $q=0$, i.e. the unit-class identity $i^*\eta(Y)=\eta_H(Y\cap H)$, which is the same statement as the comparison $\eta(Y)=\gamma^{0,0}_{Y/X}(1)$ at the unit class. No retained source gives it in the Hodge-cohomology form; the duality form, as recorded above, is Stacks' Lemma 48.7.1 on printed p. 4100, its specialisation on printed p. 4111 and Section 48.10 on printed p. 4107, with the trace identified at Lemma 50.24.3 on printed p. 4274 --- but with one qualification found since and worth stating here: Lemma 48.10.2, the isomorphism of that section, is proved for $f$ flat, and in the square of the base change both maps are closed immersions, so the lemma does not apply as it stands. What applies is the criterion of Lemma 48.10.1 on the same printed page, which reduces the question to $Lj^*R\mathcal H om_{\OO_X}(\OO_H,\omega^\bullet_X)\cong R\mathcal H om_{\OO_Y}(\OO_Z,Lj^*\omega^\bullet_X)$ for two transverse closed immersions, with Lemma 48.10.3 on the same page as the tool. In ordinary language that is the statement that a Koszul resolution of $\OO_H$ restricts, along $j$, to a Koszul resolution of $\OO_Z$ in $\OO_Y$ --- which is the transversality hypothesis itself, made derived. That is the precise gap: not a missing theorem of duality, and not a missing computation, but a compatibility that has to be written out in whichever language one works in. Also checked in this pass, closing the transcription question: the two remaining solution files on the machine, `gh-nilaykumar-hartshorne.tex` (Chapter I and II only, up to II.2.7) and `gh-btg-hartshorne.org` (108 lines of notes on Chapter 1), contain no entry for III.7.3 or III.7.4, so every solution set held here has now been read for this exercise. **The curve case, same day.** In the criterion of the last record, $p=n-1$ gives $n-p=1$, so the products are single first Chern classes and the hypothesis reads: the image of $c:\Pic X\otimes k\to H^1(X,\Omega^1)$ of part (c) is all of $H^1(X,\Omega^1)$. For such $X$ --- in particular when that map is onto --- the comparison holds for every curve $Y\subset X$ and the base change holds for every transverse pair $(Y,H)$ with the same property in $H$. ### III.12.3 and III.11.7(a) print false claims and have no complete published solution

**Object and need.** `P-AGH3123JUMPINGIDEAL` (Hartshorne III, Ex. 12.3, printed pp. 291–292) prints a jump $h^0(t,\mathcal I)=h^1(t,\mathcal I)=1$ at $t=0$ for the ideal sheaf of a degenerating quartic curve, and `P-AGH3117NONALGSHEAF` (III, Ex. 11.7, printed p. 281) prints that the kernel of $\Pic\hat X\to\Pic Y$ is an infinite-dimensional vector space over $k$. Both cards need a published proof of the corrected statements, or the owner's acceptance of the card's own derivation.

**Observed evidence.** For 12.3, $0\to\mathcal I_t\to\OO_{\PP^4}\to\OO_{X_t}\to0$ gives $h^0(\mathcal I_t)=\ker(H^0(\OO_{\PP^4})\to H^0(\OO_{X_t}))=0$ because $H^0(\OO_{\PP^4})=k$ restricts injectively, and, $H^1(\PP^4,\OO)=0$ being zero, it gives $h^1(\mathcal I_t)=\operatorname{coker}(H^0(\OO_{\PP^4})\to H^0(\OO_{X_t}))=h^0(\OO_{X_t})-1=0$; so both printed functions are identically zero; the jump occurs for $\mathcal I(1)$, where $H^0$ is the one-dimensional kernel of $H^0(\OO(1))\to H^0(X_t,\OO(1))$ and $H^1$ the one-dimensional cokernel, both zero for $t\ne0$ because $X_t$ is the rational normal quartic. Dongryul Kim, *Solutions to Hartshorne's Algebraic Geometry*, Chapter III §12 Exercise 12.3, release PDF p. 215, revision `6c627eed7b0226249df79b8777f5ac450f17885a`, verifies the flat limit and the flatness of $\mathcal I$ and stops; the list of problems he has not solved, at the head of the text on PDF p. 1, asks "Exercise 3.12.3: The statement seems to be false?". (The inference "$H^1(\mathcal I_t)\hookrightarrow H^1(\PP^4,\OO)=0$" stood in this sentence and in the one below before 2026-11-16; it is wrong: the long exact sequence gives $H^0(\OO_{X_t})\to H^1(\mathcal I_t)\to H^1(\PP^4,\OO)=0$, so $H^1(\mathcal I_t)$ is the cokernel of $H^0(\OO_{\PP^4})\to H^0(\OO_{X_t})$ and not a subgroup of $H^1(\PP^4,\OO)$; it is replaced by that computation, which is what the card proves.) A. Egbert, *Solutions to Hartshorne's Algebraic Geometry*, III.12.3, printed p. 204, gives no mathematics and writes that the question "has a typo which makes it not quite work", citing MathOverflow question 90260, which was not used as evidence. For 11.7(a), Kim p. 213 proves surjectivity and that the successive kernels are $H^1(Y,\OO_Y(-dn))$, then asserts that the kernel itself is a $k$-vector space as an inverse limit of $k$-vector spaces; that inference is exactly the false step in characteristic $p$, where the multiplicative formal group is not additive. Egbert covers III.11 only through 11.4 (pp. 200–201).

**Impact and owner.** The cards carry the corrected statements and prove them: the jump for $\mathcal I(1)$ on 12.3 (steps s3–s5), and on 11.7 the filtered statement in every characteristic with the $k$-vector-space conclusion in characteristic zero (steps s2–s5) and an explicit characteristic-$p$ line bundle of infinite order in the kernel (step s6). What is missing is a published argument to check those against, so neither card is source-complete on the printed claim.

**Uncertainty.** Searched: all twelve retained Hartshorne solution files in `tmp/sources` (Borcherds, Cais, Cutrone–Marshburn, Egbert, Kim, Lomont, Okamoto, Park, Saglam–Chris, Sam, Stein, Troiani), by full-text extraction. Found: Chapter III §12 material only in Kim and Egbert — Kim for 12.1–12.6, Egbert for 12.1–12.5 with 12.3 a typo note and 12.6 `MISS`; no other file contains a §12 exercise. Conclusion: no complete published solution for the printed 12.3 claim, and none for the characteristic-$p$ assertion in 11.7(a). Confidence: high for these sets. Gaps: a published treatment may exist outside them; MathOverflow 90260 was cited by Egbert but not read as evidence here.

**Repair.** A source that computes the twisted cohomology of the degenerating quartic family, and one that determines the characteristic-$p$ structure of $\ker(\Pic\hat X\to\Pic Y)$; or the owner's direction to accept the card's derivations for these two statements.


**Searched outside the retained sets, III.12.3 and III.11.7(a) (issue #131, 2026-11-11).** Nothing was located for either corrected statement. The correction for 12.3 was recomputed: $0\to\mathcal I\to\OO_{\PP^4}\to\OO_{X_t}\to0$ gives $h^0(\mathcal I_t)=0$ and $h^1(\mathcal I_t)=\operatorname{coker}(H^0(\OO_{\PP^4})\to H^0(\OO_{X_t}))=h^0(\OO_{X_t})-1=0$, so both printed functions are identically zero, while for $\mathcal I(1)$ the restriction $H^0(\OO_{\PP^4}(1))\to H^0(\OO_{X_t}(1))$ is injective with $h^0=5$ on both sides for $t\neq0$ and has a one-dimensional kernel for $t=0$ because $X_0$ spans only a hyperplane, giving $h^0=h^1=1$ at $t=0$ and $0$ elsewhere. For 11.7(a) the search found only Math StackExchange question 4667761 on III.11.5, which computes the successive kernels $H^1(Y,\OO_Y(-dn))$ and does not touch the infinite-dimensionality claim.

**Step-by-step pass, III.11.7(a) (2026-11-11).** Read against the book p. 281 and Exercise II.9.6. Checked and unchanged: s1, $H^0(X_r,\OO)=k$ from $H^0(Y,\OO_Y)=k$ (I.3.4a) and the vanishing of $H^0$ of a negative-degree line bundle on a curve; s2, the square-zero Picard sequence for $\OO_Y(-rd)$ with $H^2=0$ on a curve; s3, $\Pic\hat X=\varprojlim\Pic X_r$ and $K_r/K_{r+1}=V_r$, using the surjectivity of the transition maps and its consequence for $\varprojlim{}^1$; s4, $\dim_kV_r=rd^2+d(d-3)/2$ from the hypersurface sequence and $\dim H^2(\PP^2,\OO(-m))=\binom{m-1}{2}$; s5, the characteristic-zero logarithm identifying $1+\hat{\mathcal I}$ with $\hat{\mathcal I}$, so that $K$ is a $k$-vector space containing the strictly descending chain $K_1\supsetneq K_2\supsetneq\cdots$; s7, nonalgebraizability. **One step corrected**, in the characteristic-$p$ counterexample: its coefficient comparison was written for $1+s^{2m}/t^m$, which equals $u^m$ only when $m$ is a power of $p$, while the text claimed it for every $m$. The conclusion, that no positive power of $u$ is a coboundary and $K$ is not a $k$-vector space when $\operatorname{char}k=p$, is unchanged. **The reduction this note recorded is withdrawn (2026-11-16).** It said it suffices to treat $m=p^a$, because $u^M=A/B$ implies $u^{p^aM}=A^{p^a}/B^{p^a}$; that produces a coboundary at exponent $p^aM$, and $p^aM$ is a power of $p$ only when $M$ is, so it excludes nothing. **Outside source read, III.12.3 (2026-11-16).** MathOverflow question 90260, *Trouble with semicontinuity* (asked 2012-03-05), is the thread Egbert cited, and it is the one place outside the solution sets where the corrected statement is argued. Read through the Stack Exchange API (`/2.3/questions/90260/answers?site=mathoverflow`) into the text version `tmp/sources/mo-90260-trouble-with-semicontinuity.md`, it has two substantive answers. S. Kovács (2012-03-05, with an addendum; 10 upvotes) claims $h^0(\OO_{X_0})=2$ from the nilpotent $x_2$ and hence $h^1(\PP^4,\mathcal I_0)=1$, that is, that the printed $h^1$ line is right and only the printed $h^0$ line wrong; his fibre ideal is $\mathcal J+(x_0x_2,x_1x_2,x_2^2,x_3x_2,x_4x_2)$ with $\mathcal J$ the ideal of the quartic curve in $\PP^3$, and his addendum writes the coordinate ring of $\mathscr X_0\cap U_0$ as $k[y_1,x_2]/(y_1x_2,x_2^2)$ with $y_1=x_1/x_0$, which mixes the degree-zero localization with the degree-one coordinate $x_2$; the element of that chart is $x_2/x_0$, and it is zero. The questioner makes that observation in the question body after its own edit, $x_2/x_i=x_2x_i/x_i^2=0$. That conclusion does not hold: in his ideal $x_2$ is annihilated by every coordinate, so in the localization at any $x_i$ it is zero, and a section of $\OO(1)$ vanishing on every standard affine chart is the zero section; $x_2$ is therefore not a function on $X_0$, $h^0(\OO_{X_0})=1$, and $h^1(\PP^4,\mathcal I_0)=0$. The annihilating relations are exactly those of this family: in $\ker(k[a,x_0,\ldots,x_4]\to k[a,s,u])$ with $x_0=s^4$, $x_1=s^3u$, $x_2=as^2u^2$, $x_3=su^3$, $x_4=u^4$ one has $x_2x_0=ax_1^2$, $x_2x_1=ax_0x_3$, $x_2x_3=ax_1x_4$, $x_2x_4=ax_3^2$ and $x_2^2=a^2x_0x_4$. J. Böhm (2015-05-15) computes the fibre ideal by elimination in Macaulay 2 and reports all $H^i(\PP^4,\mathcal I_0)=0$ for $i=0,\ldots,4$, which agrees; he asks for a reconciliation and gets none. The contrast that makes Kovács's reading plausible is Example III.12.9.2, printed p. 289, where the nilpotent $z$ of the cubic family has $zw\ne0$ and does give $h^0(\OO)=2$; the difference is that product. What this pass did to the card, corrected on 2026-11-16: the opening paragraph's computation $h^1(\mathcal I_t)=\operatorname{coker}(H^0(\OO_{\PP^4})\to H^0(\OO_{X_t}))=0$ replaced an incorrect "embeds in $H^1(\PP^4,\OO)=0$", and that stands. This entry also said the step's Hilbert-polynomial argument "did not exclude a nilpotent, since this family's nilpotent contributes only in degree one and leaves $P(m)=4m+1$"; that is false and is withdrawn. $Z$ and $X_0$ both have $P(m)=4m+1$, and a nonzero kernel $K$ of $\OO_Z\to\OO_{X_0}$ is a coherent sheaf on a curve with $P_K=P_Z-P_{X_0}=0$, while $K(m)$ is generated by global sections for $m\gg0$ and $H^1(\PP^4,K(m))=0$ by Serre vanishing (Theorem III.5.2, printed p. 228, in `tmp/sources/hartshorne-1977-algebraic-geometry.md` with printed p. $=$ PDF p. $-15$), so $h^0(K(m))=\chi(K(m))=P_K(m)=0$ for those $m$ and $K=0$. The vanishing step stood in neither this entry nor the card's step s1 until 2026-11-16, and both now carry it: without it $P_K=0$ does not contradict $h^0>0$. The Hilbert-polynomial argument is restored on the card as the exclusion, and the annihilator computation stays, in the remark, where it refutes the published answer. The card's conclusion is unchanged: the printed claim is false in both lines.

Cutrone–Marshburn, Chapter 4 §1 exercise 5, argues "Conversely, suppose that $h^0(K-D)=h^0(K)=g$ and $g>0$. Then $h^0(K-D)=h^0(K)$ so $D\sim0$", which does not follow: equal dimensions give only $L(K-D)=L(K)$, and the standard consequence is $\ell(P)=2$ for $P\in\operatorname{Supp}D$, hence $X\cong\PP^1$. The card's steps 5–7 supply that argument. **Sourced 2026-11-15 by the Stacks Project for $D\ne0$ only**: Lemma 53.3.5 (tag 0CCS), printed pp. 4436–4437 of version ed88ff78, gives $r\le d$ for a $g^r_d$ and, for $d>0$, that equality forces $H^1(\OO_X)=0$, proved by the divisor sequence with the equality case carried to a large power with vanishing $H^1$. **Its equality clause needs that $d>0$ and the printed statement does not carry it**: at $d=0$ the pair $(\OO_X,H^0(\OO_X))$ is a $g^0_0$ on every curve, so on a curve of genus $g>0$ one has $r=d=0$ without $g=0$, and the printed proof's step to a large power uses that $\mathcal L$ is ample, which $\OO_X$ is not. Lemma 53.10.2(1) (tag 0C6T), printed p. 4450, gives the converse for $g=0$ and likewise assumes $d>0$. Yang's Solution 4.6.9, printed p. 99, takes a nonzero section of $\mathcal I_Y\otimes\pi^*\OO_{\PP^3}(m)$ for $m\gg0$ on the blowup $\pi:\tilde\PP\to\PP^3$ of $X$ and concludes that $S=\pi(\operatorname{Supp}s)$ is a surface of degree $m$ containing $X$; nonsingularity, which is what the exercise asks for, is not discussed. His route to the section is not the printed hint's either: he takes $\pi_*(\mathcal I_Y\otimes\pi^*\OO(m))\cong(\pi_*\mathcal I_Y)(m)$ and gets a global section by "Serre's theorem", which is a global-generation statement and not Serre vanishing, and he forms no very ample system and applies no Bertini, which is what the hint points at. With $\beta=1$ that is the printed hint carried out on the blowup, but it ends at smoothness of the member in $\tilde\PP$ and does not descend to the image surface in $\PP^3$, which is what the card's s6--s8 do. The card keeps its own proof and the citation obligation stands. Third pass, 2026-11-16: step s6's reason for $\pi_*\OO(-E)=\mathcal I_X$ was a false inference. Generation of the Rees algebra in degree one does not make $\pi_*\OO(1)$ its degree-one piece; that pushforward is the Ratliff--Rush closure $\bigcup_k(\mci_X^{k+1}:\mci_X^k)$, and the counterexample $\mci=(x^4,x^3y,xy^3,y^4)\subset k[x,y]$, where $x^2y^2\mci\subseteq\mci^2$ and $x^2y^2\notin\mci$, is recorded on the card. The step now argues from normality: $\PP^3$ is normal, so $\pi_*\OO=\OO$ by Stein factorization (Corollary III.11.5, printed p. 280 of `tmp/sources/hartshorne-1977-algebraic-geometry.md`), and $\pi_*\OO(-E)$ is then an ideal containing $\mathcal I_X$ and contained in $\sqrt{\mathcal I_X}=\mathcal I_X$.

### IV.3.11(a) — published sources cite Shafarevich instead of proving it

**Object and need.** `P-AGH4311PROJECTIONCLOSEDIMMERSION`, Hartshorne IV Ex. 3.11(a): for a nonsingular variety $X\subseteq\PP^n$ of dimension $r$ with $n>2r+1$, exhibit $O\notin X$ whose projection induces a closed immersion into $\PP^{n-1}$.

**Observed evidence.** A. Egbert, *Solutions to Hartshorne's Algebraic Geometry* (2013), IV.3.11, printed p. 223 (entry 4.3.20), gives the whole of part (a) as "This is Shafarevich Algebraic Geometry 1, theorem 9, page 136" — a citation, not an argument. His entry 4.3.21 then proves part (b), the Veronese secant-variety computation, in full. Park and Lomont do not reach IV.3; the remaining retained sets contain no IV.3 exercise.

**Impact and owner.** The card's own proof of (a) is complete: separate points and tangent vectors by a projection center outside the corresponding proper closed loci, the dimension count $n>2r+1$ guaranteeing the center exists, then (II, 7.3) for the closed immersion. That derivation is not a published solution, so the obligation stays open under #102 alongside III.7.4(b),(d), IV.4.22 and IV.6.9.

**Uncertainty.** Searched: Egbert, Park, Lomont, Saglam–Chris, Cais, Sam, Cutrone–Marshburn, Borcherds, Stein, Kim (Chapters I–III only). Found: the Shafarevich citation, and Egbert's full treatment of (b). Conclusion: no complete published proof of (a) among them. Confidence: high. Gaps: Shafarevich's Theorem 9 itself was not consulted; it is a reference in another book, not an exercise solution.

**Repair.** A complete published solution of IV.3.11(a), or the owner's direction to accept the card's derivation for that part.

**Transcription, 2026-11-16: IV.3.11(a) is transcribed from Shafarevich, and (b) has no published proof of the clause it prints.** Read for this: I. R. Shafarevich, *Basic Algebraic Geometry 1*, third edition (2013), §5.4 "Projective Embedding of Nonsingular Varieties", text version `tmp/sources/shafarevich-2013-basic-algebraic-geometry-1-pp129-138.md`, at Theorem 2.25 (printed p. 134), the lemma on isomorphic embeddings (printed pp. 134--135), Corollary 2.7 (printed p. 135) and the proof of Theorem 2.25 (printed pp. 135--136), whose folios were fixed against the PDF, where printed p. $N$ is PDF p. $N+16$; and A. Egbert, *Solutions to Hartshorne's Algebraic Geometry* (2013), entries 4.3.20 and 4.3.21, printed p. 223, text version `tmp/sources/hartshorne-solutions-egbert.md`. Published and now transcribed at the card's steps: (a) in full, the two incidence varieties with their dimensions, the choice of the centre, the lemma on isomorphic embeddings with Shafarevich's Nakayama proof, and Corollary 2.7 with its one-line proof. **The part with no published proof** is the clause of (b) that *every* point of *every* secant line of the Veronese surface lies on infinitely many secant lines: Egbert's 4.3.21 argues it for a general point, in his words "If $r\in\PP^5$ is a general point on a secant line $\overline{v(P)v(Q)}$ of $X$, then $\overline{pq}$ maps to a conic $C$ in $X$ and $r$ then lies on the plane spanned by $C$. Any other line on the plane passing through $r$ is also a secant line to $C$ and thus to $X$. Thus a general point on a secant line to $X$ lies on a one-dimensional family of secant lines to $X$", and he does not treat the points of a secant line that his generality excludes, among them the points of the conic $C$ itself. The card's steps `veronese-conic` and `infinitely-many-secants` prove the clause for an arbitrary point, by the degree-two projection of the conic from that point, and those steps are the card's own. Two things are not read: Shafarevich's Theorem 1.15, which Corollary 2.7 cites for the finiteness of the projection, and his Theorem 1.25, which the dimension count cites, the retained copy holding printed pp. 129--138 only. **Correction, 2026-11-16, on the reader's report of #121: the IV.3.11 record.** The record above was rewritten in place by commit `bf46084e5c` and is restored here to the text it carried on its date, as `970c2227aa` introduced it; it then read that (a) was "published in full", "the two incidence varieties with their dimensions". Four corrections follow, all of this date.

- **Part (a) is published in full, and the bound the card needs is Harris's.** J. Harris, *Algebraic Geometry: A First Course* (1992), Lecture 11, Proposition 11.24, states that the secant variety $S(X)$ of an irreducible $k$-dimensional variety $X\subset\PP^n$ is irreducible of dimension at most $2k+1$, with equality if and only if the general point on a secant line lies on only finitely many secant lines, and his note that "in this statement we need only consider points $p$ lying on honest secant lines, that is, secant lines actually spanned by points of $X$". Its Example 11.22 gives the dimension $2k$ of the variety of secant lines that the count uses, through the secant line map $s\colon X\times X-\Delta\to\mathbb G(1,n)$, and the proposition takes the incidence correspondence of pairs $(l,p)$ with $p\in l$ over that variety, so that $\dim\Sigma=2k+1$ and $\dim S(X)\le2k+1$: the honest secant lines and not the pairs with equal entries. So (a) is answered by Shafarevich together with Harris, the secant bound from the proposition, the tangent bound, the lemma on isomorphic embeddings and Corollary 2.7 from Shafarevich. Read at Example 11.22, the incidence display before Proposition 11.24, Proposition 11.24 and the Veronese paragraph after Exercise 11.25, in the text version `tmp/sources/harris-1992-algebraic-geometry-first-course-pp128-149.md`; that version carries no printed folios, so the page of those statements is not established, and it lies within printed pp. 128--149, the range the version retains.
- **Shafarevich's secant count is defective as printed.** His $\Gamma$ is the set of triples $(a,b,c)$ of $\PP^N\times X\times X$ with $a,b,c$ collinear; for $b=c$ the three points $a,b,b$ lie on a line for every $a$, so $\Gamma$ contains $\PP^N\times\Delta_X$, whose image under $\varphi$ is all of $\PP^N$, of dimension $N>2n+1$. Hence the printed identity $U_1=\varphi(\Gamma)$ makes $U_1$ the whole ambient space and the printed bound $\dim U_1\le\dim\Gamma=2n+1$ false of the set he identifies with $U_1$, so it bounds nothing about centres. The points lying on a line through two distinct points of $X$ are the image of the part with $b\ne c$, which the printed passage neither separates from the diagonal nor bounds. The restored record's "the two incidence varieties with their dimensions" is wrong about this one, and the secant bound is the one (a) needs.
- **The card.** Step `secants` now proves the bound: Harris's Proposition 11.24, with the card's own incidence variety over the complement of the diagonal, written before this batch, deleted by commit `9a5cd235da` and restored to the step, marked there as the card's own. The erratum about Shafarevich's count and the provenance sentences that stood inside the solution are in the remark on the published solution. The clause of (b) that the restored record calls unpublished is unchanged: Egbert's 4.3.21 and Harris's Example 11.22 both argue it for a general point of a secant line, and the card's steps `veronese-conic` and `infinitely-many-secants` prove it for every point of every secant line, as the card's own.
- **Not read:** Shafarevich's Theorem 1.15, which Corollary 2.7 cites for the finiteness of the projection, and his Theorem 1.25, which the dimension count cites, the retained copy holding printed pp. 129--138 only; the rest of Harris's Lecture 11, and any other lecture of that book. Harris's Example 11.22 also gives (b)'s dimension, $\dim S(X)=4$, from the same conic in the plane through the point and from the cones over $S(X)$ with vertex a point of it.

A proof would run by induction on the length of the word, pulling a terminal collinearity back through the last quadratic transformation, where a target line meets the inverse images of the three target base points as a conic, and would need the induction hypothesis for incidences with curves of every degree; that is not written out. ### II.2.15(c) is closed on Haiman's Theorem 8.8

**Object and need.** `P-AGH2215VARTOSCH` (Hartshorne II, Ex. 2.15(c), printed p. 81) needs a published proof that $\Hom_{\Var_k}(V,W)\to\Hom_{\Sch_k}(t(V),t(W))$ is surjective: that every morphism of the associated $k$-schemes is $t(f)$ for a morphism of varieties $f$.

**Observed evidence.** Dongryul Kim, *Solutions to Hartshorne's Algebraic Geometry*, Chapter II §2, Exercise 2.15, PDF pp. 16--17, source revision `6c627eed7b0226249df79b8777f5ac450f17885a`, proves (a) and (b) and for (c) writes: "For surjectivity, we need to show that every $f\colon t(V)\to t(W)$ actually comes from $f_c\colon V\to W$. At the level of maps, we see that $f\colon t(V)\to t(W)$ has to send $V\to W$ by part (b). This is indeed a map of varieties, if we look at the corresponding affine charts." The step from a set map on closed points to a morphism of varieties is asserted there, not proved, and the agreement of the scheme morphism with that variety morphism away from the closed points is not addressed. A. Egbert, same exercise, printed p. 76, entry `2.2.25 c.`, gives two lines: "For regularity of $\phi$, let $\phi(P)=Q$ and choose $U=\Spec A\ni p$. Then $p\in U'=\operatorname{spec}A'\subset f^{-1}(U)$. Thus $f|_{U'}\colon\Spec A'\to\Spec A$ is induced by the map on rings, and this gives regularity." Cais covers Chapter 2 §2 exercises 2.1--2.11, 2.13, 2.14 and 2.16--2.19 and has no 2.15. Park stops at 2.13 and prints bare headers `2.14.`--`2.19.` after it. Saglam--Chris states 2.15 in full and solves only (a) and (b), passing directly to 2.16.

**Impact and owner.** The card's own proof of (c) is complete and was read: closed points of $t(V)$ are the points with residue field $k$; a $k$-morphism carries them to closed points of $t(W)$; the induced set map is continuous; and at each point, after choosing affine neighbourhoods with $f(V_0)\subseteq W_0$, the morphism is the affine-variety morphism attached to a single $k$-algebra map $B\to A$, whence it is regular and $t(f)=F$. What was missing is a published argument to check it against, so II.2 was not source-complete on 2.15(c) until the argument of Haiman's Theorem 8.8 was located and transcribed; see the note at the end of this entry.

**Uncertainty.** Searched: all twelve retained Hartshorne solution files in `tmp/sources` (Borcherds, Cais, Cutrone--Marshburn, Egbert, Kim, Lomont, Okamoto, Park, Saglam--Chris, Sam, Stein, Troiani) by full-text extraction. Found: the two sketches quoted above and nothing else; Borcherds and Troiani stop at Chapter I, Stein begins at II.2.14 and does not treat 2.15, Cutrone--Marshburn covers only 2.1--2.9, Sam covers II.1.1--II.1.8, Lomont only II.1.16(b), and Okamoto only II.9. Conclusion: no complete published solution of 2.15(c) among them. Confidence: high for these sets. Gaps: a published treatment may exist outside them; it has not been located.

**Repair.** A published proof of Hartshorne II, Ex. 2.15(c), checked against the card, or the owner's direction to accept the card's derivation.

**Searched outside the retained sets (issue #131, 2026-11-11); closed 2026-11-16.** Mark Haiman, *Varieties as Schemes* (Math 256, Berkeley, March 2019), text version `tmp/sources/haiman-varieties-as-schemes.md` beside the PDF `tmp/sources/haiman-varieties-as-schemes.pdf`, Theorem 8.8 on PDF p. 18 with the proof in 8.10 on PDF pp. 18--19, gives a functorial equivalence between classical varieties over an algebraically closed field and reduced algebraic schemes over them, hence the bijection of Hom sets that II.2.15(c) asks for. The notes carry no printed folio, so PDF pages are cited. ### II.3.15 has no complete published solution in the sets inspected

**Object and need.** `P-AGH2315GEOMIRRED` (Hartshorne II, Ex. 3.15(a) and (b), printed p. 93) needs a proof that the three conditions of (a) are equivalent --- $X\times_k\bar k$ irreducible, $X\times_k k_s$ irreducible, and $X\times_k K$ irreducible for every extension field $K$ of $k$ --- and that the three conditions of (b) are equivalent --- $X\times_k\bar k$ reduced, $X\times_k k_p$ reduced, and $X\times_k K$ reduced for every extension field $K$ of $k$. Irreducibility of $X$ itself is not one of the six conditions and implies none of them. For the three of (a), $X=\Spec\CC$ over $k=\RR$ is irreducible, while $X\times_k\bar k=\Spec(\CC\otimes_\RR\CC)$ has two points. For the three of (b), $X=\Spec k[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^2)$ is irreducible over any field $k$, while $\OO(X\times_kK)=(k[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^2))\otimes_kK$ carries the nonzero nilpotent $\varepsilon\otimes1$ for every extension field $K$ of $k$, so none of those three holds either. The hard implication in (a) is (ii) $\Rightarrow$ (iii).

**Observed evidence.** Dongryul Kim, *Solutions to Hartshorne's Algebraic Geometry*, Chapter II §3, Exercise 3.15, PDF pp. 26--27, source revision `6c627eed7b0226249df79b8777f5ac450f17885a`, reduces a reducible $X_K$ to an affine chart with $A\otimes_kK$ reducible and then writes: "Now if we look at the conditions on the coefficients of $f_1, f_2, h_j$ and entries of $a_1, a_2$, it is a polynomial condition. By Nullstellensatz, this has closed points over $K$ if and only if the corresponding variety is nonempty, and this can be tested on any algebraically closed field. So it will have a closed point over $k$ as well. Since we need only a finite number of coefficients, we may even assume that $K$ is a finite extension of $k$." That last passage does not follow: $k$ is separably closed, not algebraically closed, and a finite purely inseparable extension $L/k$ of a separably closed but non-perfect $k$ need not have a $k$-point — $\Spec k[x]/(x^p-u)$ has none when $u\notin k^p$, although it has one over $k(u^{1/p})$. Cais, Exercise 3.15(a), proves "(i) $\Rightarrow$ (iii)" by arguing that a zero divisor in $A\otimes_kK$ is a system of equations with coefficients in $k$ having a solution over $K$, and that the Nullstellensatz then gives one over $k$; that would show that $A\otimes_kK$ is a domain whenever $A$ is, which fails in characteristic $p$: for algebraically closed $k$ of characteristic $p$, $A=k[x,y]/(y^p-x^p-x)$ is a domain (since $x^p+x\notin k(x^p)=k(x)^p$) and $A\otimes_k\Frac(A)\cong K[x,y]/((y-s)^p)$ with $s^p=x^p+x$ has the nonzero nilpotent $y-s$. Saglam--Chris print (a) and (b) as "To be done"; Egbert's entry `2.3.31` reads "See Liu, section 3.2.2", and Cutrone--Marshburn's II.3 exercise 15 reads "See 'Algebraic Geometry and Arithmetic Curves' by Qing Liu section 3.2.2 pg 89". Park covers Chapters I and IV, Stein's homework covers II.2, Cais stops at 3.15, and Okamoto covers II.9.

**Impact and owner.** The card proves the two reductions itself: an algebraic purely inseparable base change is a universal homeomorphism, so (ii) $\Leftrightarrow$ (i); and extension of scalars over an algebraically closed field preserves the set of minimal primes, so (i) $\Rightarrow$ (iii). The equivalence of the four conditions is the Stacks Project, Lemma 10.47.3 (Tag 037K), and the second reduction is Lemma 10.47.2; the card cites both by tag and records the characteristic-$p$ example showing why irreducibility cannot be tested through domain-ness. What is missing is a published argument to check those steps against, so II.3 is not source-complete on 3.15.

**Uncertainty.** Searched: all twelve retained Hartshorne solution files in `tmp/sources` (Borcherds, Cais, Cutrone--Marshburn, Egbert, Kim, Lomont, Okamoto, Park, Saglam--Chris, Sam, Stein, Troiani) by full-text extraction. Found: the passages quoted above and nothing else. Conclusion: no complete published solution of 3.15(a) or (b) among them. Confidence: high for these sets. Gaps: Liu, *Algebraic Geometry and Arithmetic Curves*, §3.2.2 p. 89 is cited by Egbert and by Cutrone--Marshburn as the place where 3.15 is done, and is not among the retained files; it was not consulted.

**Repair.** A published proof of 3.15(a) and (b), checked against the card, or the owner's direction to accept the Stacks citation as the proof of the implication (ii) $\Rightarrow$ (iii).

**Closed, 2026-11-16.** The card's two parts are now the Stacks Project's proof transcribed rather than cited, with the printed pages of the retained compiled book `tmp/sources/stacks-project-book.pdf` (whose PDF page is its printed page). Step `affine-irreducibility-tfae` is Algebra Lemma 10.47.3 (tag 037K, printed pp. 544--545) in full, including the going-down step (10.39.19, printed p. 525), the purely inseparable homeomorphism (10.46.7, tag 0BRA, printed p. 541) and the algebraically closed tensor step (10.47.2, tag 00I7, printed p. 544); steps `xbark-irred-implies-xk-irred` and `xks-irred-implies-xbark-irred` are the proof of Lemma 33.8.9 (tag 038I, printed pp. 2832--2833) with Lemma 33.8.8 (tag 038H, printed p. 2832); step `affine-reducedness-tfae` is the first two paragraphs of Lemma 33.6.4 (tag 035X, printed p. 2821); step `purely-inseparable-reducedness-tests` is Algebra Lemma 10.44.4 (tag 030V, printed pp. 537--538) with its own cited lemmas 10.43.4 (p. 534), 10.42.4 (p. 532), 10.43.6 (tag 030U, p. 534), 10.43.7 (p. 535) and 10.44.2 (p. 536) quoted by number and page. **Correction, 2026-11-16, on the second reader's report of #121: the II.3.15 heading and its observed evidence.** Commit `89d13d01e1` also rewrote in place the section heading above, which read that II.3.15 has no complete published solution in the sets inspected, and the Observed-evidence paragraph under it. Both are restored here to the text they had on their date, and the closure of the section stands where that commit put it, in the closed paragraph and the correction that precede this record. The counterexample in the restored paragraph is false, and this record supersedes it: over an algebraically closed $k$ no such example exists, $k$ being perfect, and the nilpotent claimed does not arise there, because in $A\otimes_k\Frac(A)$ the symbols $x$ and $y$ are the images of the two generators and $s$ is a different element, so $(y-s)^p=y^p-c$ for a constant $c$ and not the relation $y^p-x^p-x$, which is squarefree. The example that Cais's step needs is over a field that is not perfect: for $k=\FF_p(u)$ the ring $A=k[x]/(x^p-u)$ is a field, and $A\otimes_kA\cong A[x]/((x-\alpha)^p)$, with $\alpha$ the image of $x$ in $A$, has the nonzero nilpotent $x-\alpha$. Irreducibility of $A$ need not survive scalar extension even over a perfect field that is not algebraically closed, $A=\CC$ over $k=\RR$ giving $\CC\otimes_\RR\CC\cong\CC\times\CC$. What the paragraph concludes is unaffected: the implication (i) $\Rightarrow$ (iii) needs the Stacks Project's route, irreducibility tested over a separable algebraic closure (Lemma 33.8.9, tag 038I) with the finite separable extensions reduced to the affine case by Algebra, Lemma 10.47.3 (tag 037K), and no Nullstellensatz over $k$. No page or source was re-read in this pass.

**Correction, 2026-11-16, on the third reader's report of #121: which step of Cais's 3.15(a) the examples address.** The record above attributes to Cais's (i) $\Rightarrow$ (iii) step a correction that belongs to an earlier one, and draws a conclusion the source does not support. In `tmp/sources/hartshorne-solutions-cais.md`, line 309 is the (ii) $\Rightarrow$ (i) step, and it reduces that step to the assertion that if $A$ is a domain then so is $A\otimes_kK$ for a purely inseparable extension $K/k$. That assertion is false: for $k=\FF_p(u)$ the ring $A=k[x]/(x^p-u)$ is a field, since $u\notin k^p$, and with $K=A=k(u^{1/p})$ the tensor is $A\otimes_kA\cong A[x]/((x-\alpha)^p)$ with $\alpha$ the image of $x$ in $A$, whose nonzero element $x-\alpha$ satisfies $(x-\alpha)^p=0$. The example is therefore a counterexample to the reduction at line 309, and to the general claim that a zero divisor of $A\otimes_kK$ forces one in $A$; it is not a statement about the (i) $\Rightarrow$ (iii) step. That step is at line 313, and it invokes the proposition proved at line 311, which is stated for an extension $k'/k$ with $k$ algebraically closed and argued by the Nullstellensatz, the source writing "crucially using that $k$ is algebraically closed"; the exercise as printed, text version `tmp/sources/hartshorne-1977-algebraic-geometry.md`, opens "Let X be a scheme of finite type over a field k (not necessarily algebraically closed)". The defect of the (i) $\Rightarrow$ (iii) step is the hypothesis of the proposition it invokes, and the step is unjustified as written for a base field that is not algebraically closed. The claim in the record above that (i) $\Rightarrow$ (iii) "needs the Stacks Project's route" is withdrawn: the proposition's hypothesis fails at $k$ and not at $\bar k$, so what the passage shows is where the step stops, not that the equivalence requires the route by which the closed paragraph below proves it. The Observed-evidence paragraph of this entry carries the same attribution and is left as it stands. Not checked: whether a repair of that step taken inside the source's own method exists, and Cais's 3.15(b) beyond the lines read for the report.

### II.3.10(b) is false as printed in characteristic 2, and the retained solutions repeat it

**Object and need.** `P-AGH2310FIBRES` (Hartshorne II, Ex. 3.10(b), printed p. 92): for $X=\Spec k[s,t]/(s-t^2)$, $Y=\Spec k[s]$ and $a\neq0$, "show that the fibre $X_y$ consists of two points, with residue field $k$", under the sole hypothesis that $k$ is algebraically closed.

**Observed evidence.** In characteristic $2$ the Frobenius map of $k$ is bijective, so $a=r^2$ for some $r\neq0$ and $t^2-a=(t-r)^2$; the fibre is $\Spec k[t]/((t-r)^2)$, one nonreduced point with residue field $k$. The printed claim is false there. The retained sets repeat it without the hypothesis: Kim, PDF p. 23, writes "If $a\ne0$ then this is isomorphic to $k\times k$"; Cais, 3.10(b), writes that the fibre over $y=(s-a)$ consists of the two points $(s-a,t-\sqrt a)$ and $(s-a,t+\sqrt a)$; both need $\operatorname{char}k\neq2$.

**Impact and owner.** The card keeps the printed statement, computes the characteristic-two fibre as a step, and proves the two-point assertion with the added hypothesis $\operatorname{char}k\neq 2$; the other two assertions of (b), the fibre over $0$ and the generic fibre, hold in every characteristic.

**Uncertainty.** The counterexample is verified directly from the printed hypotheses; the printed page and the two published steps are quoted above. Confidence: high. Gaps: no erratum for this exercise was located.

**Repair.** An erratum for Hartshorne II.3.10(b), or the owner's direction to keep the card as it stands.

Read for it: Dongryul Kim, Exercise 2.3.10, PDF p. 23, text version `tmp/sources/hartshorne-solutions-kim.md`; the Cais solutions, Exercise 3.10, PDF p. 12 of 29, the file having no printed folio, text version `tmp/sources/hartshorne-solutions-cais.md`; A. Shichijo, Exercise 3.10, printed p. 7, text version `tmp/sources/shitijyou-ch2-section3.md`; A. Egbert, Exercise II.3.10, printed p. 84, text version `tmp/sources/hartshorne-solutions-egbert.md`. Published in full: part (a), by Cais, with Kim and Shichijo for the reduction and the ring computation and Shichijo for the gluing over an affine cover; the fibre over $a=0$, the fibre over $a\neq0$ and the generic fibre, by Kim, Shichijo and Egbert, and by Cais. **The part with no published proof** is the two-point assertion for $a\neq0$ under the exercise's only hypothesis, that $k$ is algebraically closed: all four sources pass from $k[t]/(t^2-a)$ to $k\times k$ without requiring the two roots to be distinct, so each proves the assertion only for $\operatorname{char}k\neq2$, and in characteristic $2$ it is false, as this entry's Observed evidence computes. The only published statement of the defect located is in the two comments named on the card, 3488648 and 3489729 on Math StackExchange 1709194, text version `tmp/sources/mse-1709194-geometric-generic-fibre-hart-ii310.md`, which record that the two-point reading needs $t^2-a$ separable and that in characteristic $2$ the fibre over $a$ is a single point of multiplicity two. Recorded from the same reading: Egbert's two idempotents carry the denominator $2\sqrt2$ where $2\sqrt a$ belongs.


**Correction, 2026-11-16, on the reader's report of #121: the two letters and the kernel in the transcription of Cais's 3.10(a).** The transcription record above of today is left as written, and the card's step `uy-homeomorphism-onto-fiber` is what changes. Cais, Exercise 3.10(a), PDF p. 12 of 29, text version `tmp/sources/hartshorne-solutions-cais.md` at lines 281 and 283, factors the projection through two maps of his own, $B\xrightarrow{\phi}B\otimes_AA_p\xrightarrow{\psi}B\otimes_A\kappa(p)$ in his letters; the card had written his $\phi$ as $\Spec\phi$ in the card's letters, and in those letters $\phi$ is already Shichijo's ring map $B\to A$, quoted three steps earlier, so one symbol named two maps. The factorized map is now $\theta$, with Cais's $\phi$ named as his. The same step wrote $\ker\psi=\mfp A$, an ideal of $A$; $\psi$ has source $A\otimes_BB_\mfp$, so its kernel is $\mfp(A\otimes_BB_\mfp)$, whose contraction to $A$ is $\mfp A=g(\mfp)A$, and the image of the composite is now read off that contraction: the primes of $A$ containing $\mfp A$ and meeting $S=g(B-\mfp)$ trivially. Both errors are the card's transcription and not Cais's, whose own letters are consistent throughout, so nothing is named as his defect.

**Correction, 2026-11-16, on the record above of this date: the contraction of the kernel is not $\mfp A$.** The record of this date that names Cais's two letters and the kernel ends by saying that $\ker\psi=\mfp(A\otimes_BB_\mfp)$ has contraction $\mfp A=g(\mfp)A$ to $A$; that identity does not hold in general and is withdrawn here, the record itself being left as written. The contraction can be strictly larger: with $B=k[s]$, $\mfp=(s)$ and $A=B[x]$, the ring $A\otimes_BB_\mfp$ is $A_s$, in which $s$ is a unit, so $\mfp(A_s)=A_s$ and its contraction is $A$, while $\mfp A=sA$ is proper. What holds, and what the card's step `uy-homeomorphism-onto-fiber` states, is the prime-level statement: a prime $\mfq\subseteq A$ with $\mfq\cap S=\emptyset$ contains the contraction of the kernel exactly when it contains $\mfp A$, because every element of $S=g(B-\mfp)$ lies outside $\mfq$. With that the composite's image is the set of primes of $A$ containing $\mfp A$ and meeting $S$ trivially, which is $\set{\mfq \st g^{-1}(\mfq)=\mfp}$, as Cais concludes. The card carries the prime-level form and no ideal-level contraction, so no text on the card changes with this record.



### II.3.20(c)--(d) are stated for the empty closed subset

**Object and need.** `P-AGH2320DIMENSION` (Hartshorne II, Ex. 3.20, printed pp. 94--95) states (c) and (d) for an arbitrary closed subset $Y\subseteq X$, with no nonemptiness hypothesis.

**Observed evidence.** For $Y=\emptyset$ the right-hand side of (c) is an infimum over the empty family of irreducible closed subsets of $Y$; with the usual conventions $\codim(\emptyset,X)=+\infty$ and $\krulldim\emptyset=-1$ the identity in (d) fails. Both statements are therefore meaningful only for nonempty $Y$.

**Impact and owner.** The card keeps the printed statement and proves it for nonempty $Y$, with a remark recording why the empty case has no content.

**Uncertainty.** A reading of the book's conventions, not a counterexample to a true statement. Confidence: high. Gaps: Hartshorne does not define $\codim$ for $\emptyset$.

**Repair.** An erratum adding the nonemptiness hypothesis, or the owner's direction to keep the card as it stands.

**Transcription, 2026-11-16: the published arguments for II.3.20(c)--(d), and the case they leave.** Read for this: Dongryul Kim, Exercise 2.3.20, PDF pp. 31--32, text version `tmp/sources/hartshorne-solutions-kim.md`, and A. Shichijo, Exercise 3.20, printed pp. 17--18, text version `tmp/sources/shitijyou-ch2-section3.md`. Published and now transcribed at the card's steps: for a nonempty $Y$, Kim reduces to $Y$ irreducible closed ("Since $\operatorname{codim}(Y,X)$ is defined as the infimum of codimension of irreducible closed subsets, it suffices to show this for $Y$ irreducible closed") and computes $\dim Y=\dim A/\mathfrak p$ and $\operatorname{codim}(Y,X)=\dim A_{\mathfrak p}$; Shichijo reads a maximal chain of primes below $\mathfrak p_Y$, localizes at $\mathfrak p_Y$ to count $\dim\mathcal O_{X,\mathfrak p_Y}$, and passes to arbitrary $Y$ by the infimum over the irreducible closed subsets of $Y$; (d) is Chapter I Theorem 1.8(b) for Shichijo and the same two computations for Kim, with Kim adding that $\dim Y$ is the maximum over the components and $\operatorname{codim}(Y,X)$ the minimum over them. **The part with no published proof** is $Y=\emptyset$: both sources take an infimum over the irreducible closed subsets of $Y$, an empty family when $Y=\emptyset$, and neither says what the identities then assert, so the printed statement needs the nonemptiness hypothesis this entry's Object records. The card proves the nonempty case and records the empty one; it does not claim a published proof for the empty case, and none was located.

### I.2.9(b) has no complete published solution for the generators of $I(\bar Y)$

**Object and need.** `P-AGH29PROJCLOSURE` (Hartshorne I, Ex. 2.9(b), printed p. 12) asks for generators of $I(Y)$ and of $I(\bar Y)$ for the twisted cubic $Y\subseteq\AA^3$, and uses the example to show that homogenizing a generating set of $I(Y)$ need not generate $I(\bar Y)$. The second request needs a proof that the three quadrics $wy-x^2$, $wz-xy$, $xz-y^2$ generate $I(\bar Y)$.

**Observed evidence.** Richard E. Borcherds, *Hartshorne, Chapter 1: Answers to exercises* (1994), Exercise 2.9, PDF p. 2, computes $\beta(x_2-x_1^2)=x_0x_2-x_1^2$ and $\beta(x_3-x_1^3)=x_0^2x_3-x_1^3$ and says only that $I(\bar Y)$ contains $x_1x_3-x_2^2$, which is not in the ideal generated by that pair; no generating set of $I(\bar Y)$ is given. William Troiani, *Hartshorne Exercise Solutions* (October 2020), Exercise 2.9, PDF p. 5, constructs $xy-wz$ in that ideal and shows it is outside the pair, then writes: "It remains to find generators for $I(\bar Y)$ but I think $I(\bar Y)=(wy-x^2,xz-y^2,xy-zw)$ works." That is a conjecture, not a proof of generation, and his later Exercise 2.16(a) is derived "assuming the postulated solution of Exercise 2.9b is correct". The quotation is the page's: `tmp/sources/hartshorne-solutions-troiani.md` loses the display in that sentence at line 214, reading "I think $-$ works". Park covers Chapter I §1 only, so it has no 2.9.

**Impact and owner.** The card proves the equality: modulo the three quadrics every element reduces to $A+xB+yC$ with $A,B,C\in k[w,z]$, the substitution $(w,x,y,z)\mapsto(s^3,s^2t,st^2,t^3)$ turns $A(s^3,t^3)+s^2t\,B(s^3,t^3)+st^2\,C(s^3,t^3)$ into a sum whose three terms have $s$-exponents in three distinct classes modulo $3$, so each vanishes and $A=B=C=0$; and the degree-two parts separate $J$ from $Q$. What is missing is a published argument to check it against, so I.2 is not source-complete on 2.9(b).

Harris's own varieties need not be irreducible and his Example 2.21 does not prove (a)'s irreducibility, so the two are separate sources. Bertram's Proposition 4.3, recorded above as closing (c) "in the category of prevarieties", is not used: his extension to subvarieties is one sentence and the display after it is false as printed, as the card records.

### I.5.5 with $p=3$, I.5.6(b), I.5.8, I.5.12(b) and I.5.13 have no complete published solution

**Object and need.** Five requests in `SRC-TEXT-HART77` §I.5 are proved on their cards without a published argument to check against: `P-AGH55NONSINGDEGD` (I.5.5, printed p. 37, in the case $p=3$ with $3\mid d$), `P-AGH56BLOWUPSING` (I.5.6(b), printed p. 37, the two nonsingular points above a node), `P-AGH58JACOBIANRANK` (I.5.8, printed p. 37), `P-AGH512QUADRICHYP` (I.5.12(b), printed p. 38, irreducibility for $r\ge2$) and `P-AGH513NONNORMALLOCUS` (I.5.13, printed p. 38).

**Observed evidence.** Richard E. Borcherds, *Hartshorne, Chapter 1: Answers to exercises* (1994), Chapter 1.5, PDF p. 7, stops at 5.5 and has no 5.6--5.15. William Troiani, *Hartshorne Exercise Solutions* (October 2020), has only 5.9 (PDF p. 16) from this section. Andrew Egbert, *Solutions to Hartshorne's Algebraic Geometry* (October 3, 2013), covers I.5 on PDF pp. 43--52, and on these five requests gives: 5.5 as "otherwise we can use $xy^{d-1}+yz^{d-1}+zx^{d-1}=0$", which is singular at $(1:1:1)$ whenever $3=0$ in $k$ and $3\mid d$, since there the value is $3$ and every partial derivative is $d$; 5.6(b) as a paragraph about the blow-up surface and tangent directions, with no statement about the two points above the node being nonsingular; 5.8 as "The hint is the answer"; 5.12(b) as "for larger $r$, any factors must be linear, but then multiplying the two factors together will create terms of higher than degree $2$", which is false of a product of two linear forms; and 5.13 as a sketch — integral closure finitely generated by $f_1,\ldots,f_n$, "$\mco_x$ is integrally closed iff the image of $f_i$ is in $\mco_x$ for all $i$", and "a finite intersection of nonempty opens is nonempty open" — whose two assertions are the content of the exercise.

**Impact and owner.** The cards keep complete proofs: 5.5 uses $x^{d-1}y+y^{d-1}z+z^d$ for $p\mid d$, whose partials $(d-1)x^{d-2}y$, $x^{d-1}+(d-1)y^{d-2}z$ and $y^{d-1}$ give $y=0$, the equation then giving $z=0$ and the second partial then giving $x=0$ (at $d=2$ it reads $x+z$, so $x=0$ needs $z=0$ first; corrected 2026-11-16, when this paragraph said the partials force $y=x=z=0$, and corrected again on the third pass, when it put $x=0$ before $z=0$); 5.6(b) proves the general node statement in Shichijo's form, transcribing his two strict transforms on the charts $V_0=\theset{y=vx}$ and $V_1=\theset{x=uy}$, the two points $P_1=(0,0)\times(b:a)$ and $P_2=(0,0)\times(d:c)$ of the exceptional divisor and the rank-two Jacobian at each --- and supplying the $V_1$ chart that the source omits; 5.8 proves the three components of the printed hint; 5.12(b) proves the two implications through the normal form $x_0^2+\cdots+x_r^2$, from the reducibility of $x_0^2$ and $x_0^2+x_1^2$ for $r<2$ and, conversely, from the two cases of a product of two linear forms, which is $y_0y_1$ when they are independent and $c\ell^2$ when they are proportional, giving $z_0^2+z_1^2$ and $x_0^2$ respectively, that is $r=1$ and $r=0$; 5.13 identifies the nonnormal locus with the support of the finite module $\overline A/A$. What is missing is a published argument to check each against.

### I.6.6(c) is closed on Milne; the converse half of I.6.7 has no complete published solution

**Object and need.** Two requests in `SRC-TEXT-HART77` §I.6 are proved on their cards without a published argument to check against: `P-AGH66AUTP1` (I.6.6(c), printed p. 46), that every $k$-automorphism of $k(x)$ is a fractional linear transformation, and `P-AGH67PUNCTUREDLINE` (I.6.7, printed p. 47), the question "Is the converse true?" following $r=s$.

**Observed evidence.** Richard E. Borcherds, *Hartshorne, Chapter 1: Answers to exercises* (1994), Chapter 1.6, PDF p. 8, argues 6.6(c) by "if $f$ or $g$ have degree greater than 1 then $g(y)a=f(y)$ will usually have more than one solution for $y$", which is not an argument and misstates the equation ($f$ and $g$ are the coprime numerator and denominator of the image of $x$, so the equation to solve is $f(y)=a\,g(y)$); Andrew Egbert, *Solutions to Hartshorne's Algebraic Geometry* (October 3, 2013), PDF p. 55, writes "injectivity of $\phi$ $\Rightarrow$ $f,g$ are linear", and Joe Cutrone and Nick Marshburn, *Algebraic Geometry by Robin Hartshorne: Solutions*, PDF p. 25, write "if $\deg g,\deg f>1$, the map won't be injective". The inference is the content of the request and no set proves it. On 6.7 the same three sets answer $r=s$ and then give the threshold for the converse as $r\le3$ (Borcherds: "the converse is true if and only if $r\le3$"; Egbert: "the converse is only true for $r\le3$"; Cutrone--Marshburn: "the converse is not true for $r>3$"). That threshold is one too high: the extension of an isomorphism $\AA^1\setminus P\to\AA^1\setminus Q$ to an automorphism of $\PP^1$ carries the $(r+1)$-point set $\{\infty\}\cup P$ onto $\{\infty\}\cup Q$ --- the image of $\infty$ is whichever point of that set it is, and need not be $\infty$ --- and for $r=3$ the cross ratio of these four-point sets obstructs the converse, so the threshold is $r\le2$. Cutrone--Marshburn add that "any isomorphism between $\PP^1$ and $\PP^1$ fixes at most 2 points, so if $r>3$, the map must be the identity isomorphism"; the premise is true of a non-identity automorphism, but the inference is not, since an isomorphism carrying one of the two $(r+1)$-point sets to the other need not fix any of its points.

**Impact and owner.** Both cards keep complete proofs. 6.6(c) is Milne's argument transcribed since 2026-11-16 --- steps `degree-of-a-rational-function` (Lemma 9.24, printed p. 118) and `field-automorphism-fractional-linear` (Example 9.25, printed p. 119), text version `tmp/sources/milne-fields-and-galois-theory.md` --- and the card's earlier route, an automorphism fixing $\infty$ reduced to a $k$-algebra automorphism of $k[x]$ and $\deg x=\deg(q\circ p)$, was removed at `5ff1108be9` and is recorded only as the card's earlier one. 6.7's converse is settled by the four-point sets $\{\infty,0,1,\lambda\}$ and $\{\infty,0,1,\mu\}$ with $\mu$ outside the six cross-ratio transforms of $\lambda$, which exist because $k$ is infinite; step `converse-fails` now proves the invariance of the cross ratio and its six-value orbit from the one fact it needs, that an element of $\PGL(1)$ fixing $\infty$, $0$ and $1$ is the identity. What is missing is a published argument for the converse of 6.7.

### I.7.7(b) and the quadric half of I.7.8 have no complete published solution

**Object and need.** Two requests in `SRC-TEXT-HART77` §I.7 are proved on their cards without a published argument to check against: `P-AGH77CONEDEGDROP` (I.7.7(b), printed p. 55), that the join $X$ of a nonsingular point $P$ with a variety $Y^r$ of degree $d>1$ has $\deg X<d$; and `P-AGH78DEGTWOSPAN` (I.7.8, printed p. 55), that a variety $Y^r\subseteq\PP^n$ of degree $2$ sits in a linear subspace of dimension $r+1$ **and** is a quadric hypersurface there.

**Observed evidence.** For I.7.7(b) all three sets that reach the section take the printed induction on $\dim Y$. Andrew Egbert, *Solutions to Hartshorne's Algebraic Geometry* (October 3, 2013), Exercise I.7.7, PDF p. 58, writes "by Thm 7.7, 7.6b, $\deg X\cap H=\deg X$. By induction $\deg X\cap H\le\deg Y\cap H\le\deg Y=d$"; Joe Cutrone and Nick Marshburn, *Algebraic Geometry by Robin Hartshorne: Solutions*, PDF p. 27, writes "choose a hyperplane $H$ through $P$ not containing $Y$ so that the intersection multiplicity along any component of $X\cap H$ is $1$. Then by Thm 7.7 and 7.6(b), $\deg X\cap H=\deg X$". Both identities are steps of the induction and neither is proved. Richard E. Borcherds, *Hartshorne, Chapter 1: Answers to exercises* (1994), Exercise 7.7, PDF pp. 9--10, states the genericity the argument needs — a generic hyperplane through $P$ meeting $Y$ and $X$ transversely, and $X\cap H$ irreducible — and refers the second of these to remark III.7.9.1 with Bertini (II, 8.18), which is quoted rather than applied; his induction also has to know that $X\cap H$ is the cone on $Y\cap H$, which holds only when the section is the join of the same vertex with $Y\cap H$. For I.7.8 all three prove the linear span and stop: Borcherds "applying 7.7 to $Y^r$ shows that $Y$ is contained in a degree $1$ variety $H$ of dimension $r+1$ in $\PP^n$, which by 7.6 is a linear variety and therefore isomorphic to $\PP^{r+1}$"; Egbert and Cutrone--Marshburn the same with the two exercise references. The second sentence of the printed exercise, that $Y$ is a quadric hypersurface in that span, is asserted by all three and proved by none.

**Impact and owner.** Both cards keep complete proofs. I.7.7(b) is proved without the induction: blowing up the nonsingular point $P$, the resolved projection $\widetilde\rho:\widetilde Y\to Z$ onto the cone's base $Z$ is generically finite of some degree $\delta\ge1$, and $\widetilde\rho^*\OO_Z(1)\cong\OO_{\widetilde Y}(\beta^*H-E)$ gives $(\beta^*H-E)^r=\delta\deg Z$, while $(\beta^*H-E)^r=H^r+(-1)^rE^r=d-1$ because $E\cong\PP^{r-1}$ with normal bundle $\OO(-1)$; hence $\deg X=\deg Z=(d-1)/\delta\le d-1$. I.7.8 is then completed by codimension one in $L\cong\PP^{r+1}$: the homogeneous coordinate ring of $L$ is a unique factorization domain, so the prime ideal of $Y$ is generated by one irreducible homogeneous form, of degree $2$ by I.7.6(d).

Found: Chapter I §7 material only in Borcherds (PDF pp. 9--10), Egbert (PDF pp. 55--58) and Cutrone--Marshburn (PDF pp. 25--27). Troiani's Chapter I stops at §5; Park's at §1; Sam's Chapter I, after reversing its mirrored text layer line by line, at §4; Cais, Kim, Lomont, Okamoto, Saglam--Chris and Stein begin at Chapter II. That proposition says only that the degree of a nonempty $Y$ in $\PP^n$ is a positive integer; a point has degree $1$ because its Hilbert polynomial is the constant $1$, and $0!=1$. Step `blowup-resolves-projection` of `P-AGH77CONEDEGDROP` and its 2026-11-16 event say so.

**2026-11-16: I.7.7(b) is closed on Mumford's Proposition 2.5 and Harris's Example 18.16.** `P-AGH77CONEDEGDROP` now proves the degree drop from two printed statements and no longer from its own blow-up. Harris, *Algebraic Geometry: A First Course* (1992), Example 18.16, printed pp. 234--235, gives the degree of the cone over a variety as the degree of the base (printed p. 234), which with the projection from $P$ identifies $\deg X$ with $\deg Z$ for the base $Z$ of the cone, and gives $\deg(\overline X)=\deg(X)-1$ for the projection of a variety from one of its smooth points (printed p. 235). Mumford, *Stability of projective varieties*, L'Enseignement Mathématique 23 (1977), printed p. 55, gives the same count without Harris's standing assumption that the general line through $p$ meets $X$ only at $p$ and at one more point: Definition 2.2 defines $e_L(\mathcal I)$ as the normalized leading coefficient of $\chi(L^n/\mathcal I^nL^n)$, his examples after it identify that number with the Hilbert-Samuel multiplicity at the point when the base locus is a point, and Proposition 2.5 states $e_L(\mathcal I_A)=\deg X-\deg p_A(X)$. Applied with $A$ the hyperplanes through $P$, whose base locus on $Y$ is $\{P\}$, this gives $d=\deg Y=\deg p_A(Y)+1\ge\deg Z+1$, whence $\deg X=\deg Z\le d-1$. Text versions `tmp/sources/harris-1992-algebraic-geometry-first-course-pp224-243.md` and `tmp/sources/mumford-1977-stability-projective-varieties.md`. **The one step that no single source prints:** that $e_L(\mathcal I_A)=1$ at a nonsingular point. Mumford says only that $e_L$ is the multiplicity there, and Harris says only that a general $r$-tuple of hyperplanes through a smooth point of a variety meets it transversely at that point (printed p. 235); the card puts the two together and the step says so. Part (a) is unchanged and keeps its tangent-space route for $\dim X>r$, with KReiser's accepted answer 4656385 (question 4656099, cited by answer id) named for the two bounds it shares and for the induction on $\dim Y$ that it carries out. The blow-up computation is now a remark on the card rather than its proof, with its $(\beta^*H-E)^r=d-1=\delta\deg Z$ and the reasons for each term.

### V.1.11(a) and (b) of `SRC-TEXT-HART77` have no complete published solution; V.1.4(b) and the surface example of V.1.12 closed on transcriptions

**Object and need.** Two parts of one request in `SRC-TEXT-HART77` §V.1 are proved on the card without a published argument to check against, parts (a) and (b) of V.1.11; when this entry was opened it was three cards, and the other two are closed below: `P-AGH514LINEONSURF` (V.1.4(b), printed p. 367, PDF p. 382, a nonsingular degree-$d$ surface through a given line, every $d\ge1$), `P-AGH5111FINITEAUT` (V.1.11(a) and (b), printed p. 368, PDF p. 383, finiteness of the numerical classes of effective divisors with $D\cdot H=d$, and of the automorphisms modulo the identity component) and `P-AGH5112NUMAMPLE` (V.1.12, printed p. 368, PDF p. 383, a very ample $D$ numerically equivalent to a non-very-ample $D'$).

**Observed evidence.** For all of Chapter V the only retained set that reaches the section is Andrew Egbert, *Solutions to Hartshorne's Algebraic Geometry* (October 3, 2013), PDF pp. 254--261 for V.1; Park's *Exercises solutions* has Chapter V §5 only (PDF p. 31), Borcherds stops at Chapter I, and Cais, Cutrone--Marshburn, Kim, Lomont, Okamoto, Saglam--Chris, Stein and Troiani have no Chapter V. Egbert's V.1.4(b) reads "The fermat hypersurface $x^d+y^d+z^d+w^d=0$ contains the line $x-\sqrt[n]{\ }$" and breaks off inside the formula, so his entry is truncated and exhibits no surface at all; on that hypersurface the lines $x=\zeta y$, $z=\zeta w$ with $\zeta^d=-1$ lie on it in every degree, and only the line $x+y=z+w=0$ lies on it solely for odd $d$, since $x^d+(-x)^d=2x^d$ in even degree. His V.1.11(a) is "WLOG assume that $H$ is a very ample hyperplane of $\deg(H)=1$. For $D\cdot H=0$ this follows from nakai moishezon. Note that any such $D$ can only have finitely many components not intersecting $H$ since if $P_i\cdot H=0$, then $P_i\cdot P_j<0$ and with each additional such component, the genus, $2g-2=C\cdot C+C\cdot K\ge-2$ will decrease. ... Thus we are choosing $D$ from a finite set of a finite number of components": the components meeting $H$ and the coefficients $n_i$ are never bounded, and $P_i\cdot P_j<0$ is asserted. His V.1.12 reduces the curve case correctly and then writes "Consider a decomposable ruled surface $X$ over a curve with $p_a(C)>2$, let $H=|C_0+bf|$ ... By Fuentes-Pedreira thm 3.9, $|H|$ is very ample iff $b$ and $b+e$ are very ample": that criterion is retained now and is the right one for a decomposable surface, but he fixes no value of $e$ and never verifies that $b+e$ is very ample, so his surface example is a citation rather than an exhibit.

**Impact and owner.** The cards keep complete proofs: V.1.4(b) now carries the National Taiwan University surface $x^{d-1}z+xz^{d-1}+y^{d-1}w+yw^{d-1}$, whose partial derivatives have no common projective zero in characteristic zero, for every $d$, with the case analysis its source omits; V.1.11(a) bounds the $H^\perp$ component of every irreducible curve by adjunction and $p_a\ge0$, then uses that $\Num X$ is a lattice in $\Num X\otimes\RR$, and finally writes an effective divisor as a sum of at most $d$ elements of a finite set; V.1.12 takes $C\times\PP^1$ with $M=p_1^*L\otimes p_2^*\OO(1)$ very ample and $M'=p_1^*L'\otimes p_2^*\OO(1)$ not very ample for $L'=K_C(P+Q)$, whose difference pulls back from a degree-zero bundle on $C$, and Fuentes--Pedreira's Theorem 3.9(3) decides both. What is missing is a published argument for V.1.11(a).

**Uncertainty.** Searched: all twelve retained Hartshorne solution files in `tmp/sources` by `pdftotext -layout` extraction, plus `assets/attachments/Hartshorne_Solutions.pdf` (the Cais notes, recorded as a byte-identical duplicate by its provenance file). Found: Chapter V only in Egbert (V.1 at PDF pp. 254--261, V.2--V.6 at pp. 261 onward) and in Park for V.5 alone. Sam's mirrored text layer was reversed line by line and carries no Chapter V. Conclusion: no complete published solution for the three requests above among these sets. Confidence: high for these sets. Gaps: a published treatment may exist outside them.

**Located sources.** Algebraic Geometry II, National Taiwan University, 2020 Spring (course of Chin-Lung Wang), *Chapter V Surfaces* homework, text version `tmp/sources/ntu-ag2-chapter5.md` with its PDF `tmp/sources/ntu-ag2-chapter5.pdf`, settles one of the three and supplies the route for the second without a complete argument: V.1.4 is closed by it, V.1.11 is not, and V.1.12 is closed instead by Fuentes--Pedreira, as recorded three paragraphs below. V.1.4 is Exercise 4 (solution by Yi-Tsung Wang), printed p. 2 of that set: (a) by adjunction and (b) by the explicit surface $x^{d-1}z+xz^{d-1}+y^{d-1}w+yw^{d-1}$, whose four partial derivatives have only the zero common solution — the first complete published proof of (b), where Egbert stops inside a truncated Fermat sentence and Yang Pi-Yeh (printed p. 100) asserts the nonsingularity of a surface whose last two terms carry the opposite signs. V.1.11 is Exercise 11 (Shuang-Yen Lee), printed p. 4: its (a) is the card's route, but its displayed estimate $\sum_ic_i^2\le c_0^2+c_0k_0+2+\frac12k_0^2$ does not follow from its adjunction line, so the card's steps carry the corrected bookkeeping, and its (b) is the printed hint alone, which never proves that distinct automorphisms have numerically inequivalent graphs; Yang Pi-Yeh p. 101 never bounds the coefficients. V.1.12 is Exercise 12, printed p. 5, and Yang Pi-Yeh printed p. 102, and both are defective at the same point: each takes $D\times\PP^1$ as the very ample member, and $D\times\PP^1$ is $p_1^*D$, whose degree on a fibre $\{c\}\times\PP^1$ of $p_1$ is zero — on a fibre $C\times\{t\}$ of $p_2$ it is $\deg D=2g$ — hence it is not even ample, and neither exhibits the example. Both print $D'$, not $D_0$. The card records that defect and keeps the construction $p_1^*L\otimes p_2^*\OO(1)$. The page numbers in this entry were the PDF pages of the extraction; the printed pages are 367 and 368.

**Verified and transcribed (2026-11-16, corrected 2026-11-16).** The treatments were re-read in their text versions and checked line by line against the book. `P-AGH514LINEONSURF` carries the published argument rather than a parallel one: step `s3` uses the National Taiwan University set's $x^{d-1}z+xz^{d-1}+y^{d-1}w+yw^{d-1}$ in place of the card's earlier $xz^{d-1}+yw^{d-1}+x^d+y^d$, and step `s4` solves that set's four equations, which it states without solution. The solution is complete: the four partial derivatives are $2z$, $2x$, $2w$, $2y$ when $d=2$; for $d\ge3$, $z=0$ forces $x=0$ from the derivative in $z$, while $z\ne0$ turns $(d-1)x^{d-2}=-z^{d-2}$ and $x^{d-2}=-(d-1)z^{d-2}$ into $(d-1)^2=1$, which fails; and the same argument with $y,w$ replaces $x,z$. Characteristic zero enters only through the nonvanishing of $2$, $d-1$ and $(d-1)^2-1$. Two claims of the remark were wrong and are withdrawn: Egbert's V.1.4(b) sentence is truncated inside its formula, and the Fermat surface carries the lines $x=\zeta y$, $z=\zeta w$ with $\zeta^d=-1$ in every degree, only the line $x+y=z+w=0$ failing in even degree; and Yang Pi-Yeh's surface carries minus signs on its last two terms, so it is not the National Taiwan University set's surface.

`P-AGH5111FINITEAUT` and `P-AGH5112NUMAMPLE` keep proofs of their own, and neither is a transcription. For V.1.11 the National Taiwan University set's estimate $\sum_ic_i^2\le c_0^2+c_0k_0+2+\frac12k_0^2$ does not follow from its adjunction line, which bounds $\sum_i(c_i^2+c_ik_i)$ and reaches $\sum_ic_i^2$ only through $2\abs{c_ik_i}\le c_i^2+k_i^2$, and its (b) is the printed hint, which never proves that distinct automorphisms have numerically inequivalent graphs; the card's step `s8` supplies that step and nothing in `tmp/sources` does. For V.1.12 the card's steps `s6` and `s7` now run through Fuentes--Pedreira's criterion, with the card's direct product-embedding and fibre-restriction arguments kept beside them.

**V.1.12 closed on Fuentes--Pedreira.** Luis Fuentes and Manuel Pedreira, *The Projective Theory of Ruled Surfaces*, arXiv:math/0006204v3, text version `tmp/sources/projective-theory-ruled-surfaces.md` with its PDF `tmp/sources/projective-theory-ruled-surfaces.pdf`, Theorem 3.9(3), printed p. 18: on a decomposable ruled surface $|X_0+\mfb f|$ is very ample exactly when $\mfb$ and $\mfb+\mfe$ are. Write $X=C\times\PP^1$ as $\PP(\OO_C\oplus\OO_C)$, so that $e=0$, $X_0=C\times\{t\}$ and $f=\{c\}\times\PP^1$; then $p_1^*L\otimes p_2^*\OO(1)=X_0+Lf$, and the criterion decides the example in one step: very ampleness of $\mfb=L$ holds (the card's step `s3`) and that of $\mfb=L'=K_C(P+Q)$ fails (step `s4`). That is a complete published argument for the surface example, and it is the criterion Egbert cited without specializing. The criterion's proof rests on the paper's Corollary 2.13, printed p. 14, and that corollary is proved: its forward direction is Theorem 2.11, printed pp. 12--13, and its converse is Proposition 2.3, printed p. 8, applied to the system $|H-Pf|$ — a point at which the map fails is a base point of some $|H-Pf|$ by Theorem 2.11, and Proposition 2.3 produces $Q$ with $h^0(H-(P+Q)f)\ge h^0(H-Pf)-1=h^0(H)-3$ once $|H|$ is base-point-free. The case $Q=P$ is the tangent direction the earlier reading supposed untested. The defect this file and the V.2.12 card had recorded against Corollary 2.13, against Proposition 2.15 and against Theorem 3.9(3) is therefore withdrawn.


**Repair.** Discharged for V.1.4(b), on a transcription of the National Taiwan University set's Exercise 4, and for V.1.12, on Fuentes--Pedreira's Theorem 3.9(3) specialized to $C\times\PP^1$ with $e=0$. V.1.11(a) and (b) stay open: the National Taiwan University set's (a) estimate does not follow from its adjunction line and its (b) omits the step from finitely many numerical classes to finitely many automorphisms, so no complete published argument for either part has been located, and Yang Pi-Yeh bounds nothing in (a).

**2026-11-16, V.1.11: (b) closes on Bragg's Proof 2, and (a) still has no complete published proof.** The two sources named for this batch were read in their text versions on 2026-11-16: Math StackExchange answer 4775583 by KReiser, saved with its question as `tmp/sources/mse-4449474-hart-v111a-finite-automorphisms.md`, for (a); and Dan Bragg, "Automorphisms of curves" (2015), `tmp/sources/bragg-2015-automorphisms-of-curves.md`, Proof 2, "Intersection Theory", for (b). Bragg's Proof 2 is a complete published proof of (b) given (a): the graphs of distinct automorphisms are distinct irreducible curves, so they meet nonnegatively, while numerically equivalent graphs would meet in $\Gamma^2=2-2g<0$ by his conormal computation of the diagonal, hence $\sigma\mapsto[\Gamma_\sigma]$ is injective; and every graph meets the canonical divisor of $C\times C$ in the same $4g-4$, which he uses as the fixed ample divisor, ample for $g\ge2$ by Nakai--Moishezon since $K\cdot l=K\cdot m=2g-2>0$ and $K^2=2(2g-2)^2>0$. The card's steps `s6` to `s10` are that argument, so the step `s8` that the earlier record above says nothing in `tmp/sources` supplied is Bragg's. The answer 4775583's route to (a) is the card's, but two of its displays do not follow: its step from $-\sum_ib_i^2(D_i\cdot K+2)$ to $-d\,D\cdot K-2d^2$ replaces $b_i^2$ by $b_id$ under $D_i\cdot K$, which $b_i\le d$ licenses only when $D_i\cdot K\le0$ for every component and which fails on a surface with $K$ ample, and its closing sentence bounds $(D-E)^2$ below by an expression linear in $D$, so it describes no ellipsoid and yields no uniformity. Part (a) therefore stays open, and its bound stays the card's, through the orthogonal decomposition of $K_X$ in $H^\perp$ and the lattice $\Num X$. Uncertainty: whether a published treatment of (a) outside these two sources exists; the answer's own comment thread records that an earlier answer of its author had been withdrawn as insufficient.

**2026-11-16, V.1.11, corrected: two of the reasons recorded just above are withdrawn, and one case stays open.** The paragraph above records two failures of Math StackExchange answer 4775583. Both are wrong and are withdrawn on this date. First the direction: replacing $b_i^2$ by $b_id$ under $D_i\cdot K_X$ is the inequality $b_i^2D_i\cdot K_X\le db_iD_i\cdot K_X$, which follows from $b_i\le d$ when $D_i\cdot K_X\ge0$, not when it is at most $0$; the record has the sign the wrong way round, and the display is reached whenever $K_X$ is nef. Second the closing sentence: for fixed $E$ its right-hand side is an affine function of $D-E$, so with the intersection form negative definite on $H^\perp$ the inequality confines $D-E$ to a ball and finitely many lattice points follow; it need not depend on $E$ alone, and the record's "no ellipsoid" is wrong. What survives is one condition, now stated at the card's step `s3`: the comparison is reversed for a component $D_i$ with $D_i\cdot K_X<0$ and $b_i<d$, so that display is not reached on such a surface, and no published argument for that case was located. The card's step `s4` is its own and gives the uniform bound without the sign condition; steps `s1`, `s2`, `s3`, `s5`, `s6`, `s7` now say which are the answer's and which are the card's. Two further corrections of this round on the same card: adjunction for a possibly singular effective divisor is Exercise V.1.3(a), printed p. 366, and for a nonsingular curve Proposition V.1.5, printed p. 361, not Theorem V.1.3, which is on printed p. 358; Bragg's Proof 2 has two paragraphs, so the card's locators are the first and the second; and "both degrees being at least one" is corrected to their sum, the projection being constant on a ruling. **Open for V.1.11(a):** the case of a surface with a component of negative $K_X$-degree, which the published answer does not reach and the card proves as its own.
